narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimated an 84% likelihood that you will leave your current position — well above the 40% threshold that triggers a promotion denial. This means the decision was not based on your performance quality, but rather on factors suggesting you may not stay long enough to justify the investment in your advancement.

Three aspects of your profile drove this prediction most strongly, all pointing toward departure.

The most influential factor was that you have received other job opportunities while working here. This is notable given that only about 1 in 5 promoted employees reported the same — making this a strong signal that you may be weighing your options elsewhere.

The second most important factor was your overall years of professional experience. With 6 to 10 years across your career, you fall into a group that, combined with your other profile characteristics, the assessment associates with higher mobility. Employees granted promotions were more commonly in their earlier career stages.

Third, your relatively short tenure at this specific organization — between 1 and 5 years — further reinforced the concern. While this duration is common among promoted employees, in your case it compounded the other signals.

It is worth noting that many aspects of your profile are genuinely strong: you report high job satisfaction, strong emotional commitment, high organizational support, and recognition from your superiors.

To improve your chances, consider formally communicating your intention to stay and grow within the organization. Demonstrating long-term commitment — particularly by declining or deprioritizing external opportunities — could meaningfully shift this assessment in your favor.
